 Democrats vow to rein in Trump after midterm victory
 Updated / Thursday, 5 Nov 2026
 06:37
 Getty
 Democrat supporters celebrate after victory in the midterm elections that saw them seize control of the Senate 
 Democrats have vowed to use their resounding midterm victory to rein in US President Donald Trump, setting up two years of possible deadlock in Washington, as Mr Trump spent his first post-election appearance showing off his under-construction White House ballroom.
 A wave of anger over Mr Trump's policies, particularly the US-Iran war's role in pushing the cost of living higher, helped Democrats take the Senate, where they flipped seats in deeply Republican states for a majority of at least 54 to 44.
 Democrats also gained at least 30 seats in the House of Representatives.
 It will be the first time that Mr Trump, a Republican who also held the White House from 2017 to 2021, has had to contend with a Democratic-controlled Congress in both chambers.
 House of Representatives Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said the incoming majority will be focused on affordability and accountability.
 Hakeem Jeffries said the incoming majority will be focused on affordability and accountability 
 "We don't work for Donald Trump," said Mr Jeffries, a New York politician who is on track to become the first black speaker of the House.
 "We work for the American people. And the days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over."
 New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has emerged as a national Democratic figure since his election a year ago, released a video on social media urging his party to address the concerns of voters burdened by rising prices who want schools and roads.
 "It is not enough to simply win power. We must use it," Mr Mamdani said. "Now, it's time for us in the Democratic Party to deliver."
 'For me, it's relaxing'
 Mr Trump, who had devoted his last pre-election public appearance on Monday to talking about his renovations of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, called in reporters to show off the ballroom he is building at the White House.
 "When I get criticised, like, 'Why are you working on the White House?' I'm doing it because the White House is the ultimate symbol of America, and it's got to be pristine, it's got to be perfect," Mr Trump said. "For me, it's relaxing."
 He turned only briefly to the elections during his nearly hour-long appearance, telling reporters, "I'll get along probably with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive, but I have the power of the veto."
 Mr Trump had cast the midterm elections as a referendum on the first half of his second four-year stint in the White House, repeatedly urging his Republican base to "pretend I'm on the ballot", a message that Democratic Party leaders were happy to amplify.
 The result: voters in conservative strongholds who had propelled the president to his second term in office just two years ago swung dramatically toward the Democrats, fuelled by deep frustration over the unpopular war with Iran, anxiety over the high cost of living and anger at Mr Trump's stewardship of the country.
 In Texas, the biggest Republican-led state before Tuesday, Democrats ended a decades-long losing streak in seismic fashion, winning their first Senate seat there since 1988 and ousting three-term governor Greg Abbott.
 Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since the Great Depression nearly a century ago, and in South Carolina, a state that Mr Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024, Democrats turned aside his hand-picked Senate candidate.
 Donald Trump said he would 'probably' get along with the Democrats 
 Waiting on Alaska and Mississippi
 Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi remained uncalled as of yesterday morning, leaving open the possibility that the Democrats' majority could grow by another two seats to 56 to 44.
 Once seated in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Mr Trump's administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation.
 The Democratic Senate can block President Trump's nominees, including any US Supreme Court justices should a vacancy arise.
 The Democratic victory is fuelling questions about the longevity of the Supreme Court's two eldest justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, and the durability of its conservative majority.
 In the meantime, Republicans hold the reins and will have at least one must-pass piece of legislation ahead - a measure to fund the federal government past December - that they could use to enact conservative priorities during the so-called lame-duck period.
 The loss also upended Republicans' House leadership, with House Speaker Mike Johnson saying he would not continue to lead his caucus next year.
 Mr Trump, who is barred by the US Constitution from seeking a third term, acknowledged the war with Iran had played a role in his party's losses but stood by his decision.
 Vice President JD Vance, who may run as a Trump successor in the 2028 election, piled blame on his boss's decision to attack Iran in February.
 "The reason we lost is the war," Mr Vance wrote in a long social media post. "The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay."
 Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has become the first Muslim senator 
 A Democratic wave
 Democrats focused their campaign on corruption and affordability, blaming Mr Trump's expensive tariffs on imports and the war with Iran for driving up costs while highlighting the billions of dollars the Trump family has made since he returned to the White House.
 Republicans, led by Mr Trump, attacked Democrats for defending transgender people's rights and similar social issues, portraying them as radical and extreme.
 Voters made it clear they were more concerned with pocketbook issues.
 "This is close to an extinction-level event for Republicans," Republican Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said in public remarks analysing the results.
 The Democratic wave flooded huge swaths of the country. Republicans lost ground in 99% of the approximately 2,100 counties where most votes had been counted, according to tallies compiled by Reuters and USA Today.

 Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat from the party's rising left wing, won Michigan's open Senate seat, becoming the first Muslim elected to the chamber and defeating Mike Rogers, who entered the race with Mr Trump's backing.
 The night included other historic firsts for both parties, including the first Black woman elected governor in US history with Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms' win in Georgia and New Mexico's Deb Haaland becoming the country's first Native American woman to be elected governor.
